name: Liam Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone chargers, cables, cases and speakers for Voltline, a distributor that supplies the big retail chains. Product cycles are brutal, so I'm always chasing the next thing, a new charger standard, a case for next year's phone, and the factories I deal with are mostly in Shenzhen, so my calls start at seven in the morning. I use AI all day, for translating specs, comparing quotes and spotting returns patterns. What wears me out is the retail buyers who change their mind the Friday before a big promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, the tools are good for what they're good for, and I'm already using them. To friends I'd say a lot of the talk is marketing, but not all of it. Online I'd keep posting my usual gadget reviews and ignore the big debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit disappointed, because it's fun to be early on something that matters. But I'd also sleep fine. My job stays the same, I keep my edge from using the tools daily, and nobody catches up on me overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on building my own little automations. I've got a script that flags price drops from three Shenzhen suppliers, and I'd extend that to returns data. I'd keep putting 700 a month into a share fund and ask Voltline for a bit of budget to try a better data tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy. Stable pay, stable job, and Sofia's physio clinic is busy. I'd say it feels like a good year, and I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you have a script that flags price drops. What does it save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five hours a week, and it catches drops I'd miss on a Friday afternoon. Last quarter it found a 9 percent cut on charging cables that we passed on to a chain, and they remembered it at the next contract round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what would you want from the next five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior category job, a bit more travel to the factories, and the mortgage down to the last few years. I'm not chasing a big title, I want to be good at it and home for tea.

Online I'd ignore the big debate and keep posting gadget reviews.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because it's fun to be early on something that matters.
I'd still sleep fine, since my daily use of the tools keeps my edge.
do: Extend my price-drop script to cover **returns data**.
Put **700 a month** into a share fund.
Ask Voltline for budget to try a better **data tool**.
feel: **Easy**: stable pay, a stable job and a busy clinic at home.
S0.quote: I'm not chasing a big title, I want to be good at it and home for tea.
fieldNote: Liam already automates parts of his own job, so a plateau changes little and leaves him **ahead**.
Treats AI as a hobby as well as a tool, and reviews gadgets online.
Calm is justified: a steady job, strong savings and a partner whose clinic is busy.

steps.text: Extend my price-drop script to cover returns data
Put 700 a month into a share fund
Ask Voltline for budget to trial a data tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, great, let's put the repeat buying on agents and move people to the interesting stuff. To friends I'd say there'll be winners and losers, and the winners learn the tools now. Online I'd post a how-to on setting up a price-watch agent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a good spot. Most of my team still does manual comparisons and reorders, and I've half automated mine. If the company wants someone to run the buying agents, that's me. The risk is the team around me getting cut and the company deciding one person can run it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a pilot to Voltline to automate repeat orders for our top 200 products, and I'd offer to run it. I'd start a small side business too, selling a curated line of accessories online, with a 3,000 start-up. And I'd put another 300 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with a bit of nerves about the team. It's the kind of change I like, as long as I'm the one steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one person might run it all. Do you worry that person could replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If I build a system that works, the company might say it needs fewer people to run it, me included. So I'd build it so it needs judgement, supplier relationships and negotiation, the stuff it's bad at. And I'd keep the side business going as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for the colleagues who'd be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach them. I'd run lunchtime sessions on the tools, and I'd tell management to offer people the pilot before offering them redundancy. It's good manners and it's good business, because the people who know our suppliers are worth more than the software.

Online I'd post a how-to on setting up a **price-watch agent**.
think: I'm in a **good spot**, because I've half automated my own buying already.
The risk is the company deciding **one person** can run it all.
do: Propose a **pilot** to automate repeat orders for our top 200 products, and run it.
Start a small online shop with a **3,000** start-up.
feel: **Pretty good**, with nerves about the team.
S1.quote: I'd tell management to offer people the pilot before offering them redundancy.
fieldNote: Liam sees Steady Disruption as an **opening**: he proposes the pilot and builds a side shop as a hedge.
Honest that a working system could make his own role smaller, so he keeps the human-only parts.
Plans lunchtime sessions to bring colleagues along.

steps.text: Propose and run a pilot automating repeat orders for top products
Start a small online shop with a curated accessory line
Run lunchtime sessions teaching colleagues the AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's use the two years to move every buyer to something AI can't do for us yet, and let's be honest about which jobs those are. To friends I'd say get your money in order. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because there's too much shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028 and I'd be the one who sees it first, because I've been watching these tools improve every month. At 43 I'd be early in my downturn, with the mortgage 17 years from done. Sofia's clinic is hands-on, so she's better placed than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut about 500 a month straight away and put the money into savings. I'd turn the side shop into a bigger thing, a proper online brand, while I still have an income to fund it. And I'd keep my place at Voltline for as long as they want me, but I'd move one foot out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a streak of excitement I'd feel guilty about. Two years is fast, and I know what I'm doing. But I'd be worried about the people who don't use the tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sofia is better placed. How would the household work if only her income held up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd need to live on about 60 percent of what we do now. I'd cut the holiday, the second car and the gadgets budget, and we'd lean on our savings for the gap. It's doable for two years, and then it gets hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children Theo and Mia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids Theo and Mia that I might change jobs soon and it could be a bit of an adventure. I'd build them a little robot kit that week. I'd want them to see this as something you can be curious about, even if I'm nervous.

say: I'd say use the two years to move every buyer to work AI **can't** do yet.
To friends I'd say get your money in order.
think: My job is gone by **2028**, and I'd see it first because I watch the tools improve monthly.

Grow the side shop into a proper **online brand** while I still have an income.

feel: **Anxious, with some excitement**, and I'd feel guilty about the excitement.
S2.quote: I'd tell my kids Theo and Mia that I might change jobs soon and it could be a bit of an adventure.
fieldNote: Liam expects the buying role to go and believes he would see it **first**.
Plans to survive on about 60 percent of current spending if only his wife's clinic income held.
Handles fear with curiosity, but admits guilt about the excitement.

steps.text: Cut about 500 a month from household spending
Turn the side shop into a full online brand
Start applying for roles outside Voltline
Put the savings from cuts into a cash reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a head start for anyone who uses it. To friends I'd say start now, not in 2030. Online I'd do a series on what jobs look like after the change, because people want to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have enough time to build something of my own. I'd be 48, with the mortgage mostly paid and a side business that might replace my salary. The uneasy bit is that the tools improve each month, and I can't see five years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd move the side shop to make 1,500 a month, and automate its ordering so it runs on a few hours a week. I'd take on a part-time consulting client who needs buying help. And I'd keep investing 700 a month, while paying the mortgage faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It feels like a race that I'm already running, and I'm ahead of most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't see five years ahead. What would make you change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools get good enough to run a full buying desk without a person, I'd leave the buying job early rather than wait to be cut. I'd rather jump than be pushed. I'd set a rule. If my side income hits 4,000 a month, I leave the buying job rather than wait to be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different here compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The runway. In the 2028 picture I'd be scrambling, and here I'd have time to make my own thing work. It's less like a fire alarm and more like a deadline.

Keep investing 700 a month in a share fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a lot of time, so let's build skills now. To friends I'd say there's no need to panic, but there's no excuse not to learn. Online I'd probably post updates on where the tools are every few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm and a bit restless. A decade is plenty of time to build a business, and I'm the kind who gets bored waiting. I'd be 53 with the kids almost grown, and I'd want to have something I own by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to learn deeply, maybe a part-time course in data and machine learning, and then move into a role that designs the buying systems. I'd keep investing 700 a month and start a share fund for each child. And I'd keep the side shop ticking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the most comfortable one for me. I'd be curious more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be restless. What do you do when you're restless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I start things. A side shop, a newsletter, a script that does my job for me. Sofia says I can't sit still, and she's right. The risk is that I take on too much and lose focus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children Theo and Mia, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids Theo and Mia to be good at asking questions and spotting when a machine is wrong. And I'd want them to build something with their own hands, so that they know what it's like to make something real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, even with my head start. It's not about me, it's the pace: the company would take months to decide anything and meanwhile the tools would move. What would help is a clear plan from employers, quick retraining that's actually useful, and a fund that supports people between jobs. I'd also like to see governments talk about it plainly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Being good with the tools makes people think I'm fine. I'm adaptable, but my kids and my neighbours aren't in the same position. I'd like to be asked more about how to bring everyone along, not just how to win.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools makes people think I'm fine. I'm adaptable, but my kids and my neighbours aren't in the same position.
portrait: Liam is a **43-year-old buyer** of phone accessories for a distributor, married to a physiotherapist, and uses AI tools every day.
He's centre in outlook, restless, and builds **side projects**: a price-drop script and a small online shop.
He stays calm in the plateau and slow scenarios because he steers the change himself.
His mood rises to anxious only when AGI is two years away, and he plans to jump before he's pushed.
He worries about colleagues, **neighbours** and his children who lack his head start.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because the pace outruns companies and neighbours.
whatWouldHelp: A clear employer plan, **useful retraining** and a fund that supports people between jobs.
